newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition stands firm with protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition stands firm with protests.

text.p: Roadblocks and strikes around Bulgaria on Thursday showed protesters' firm rejection of the ruling Socialists' latest compromise offer for early elections on the 25th day of protests fuelled by an economic crisis.
Protesters blocked main roads to Greece and Turkey, strikes hit schools, factories and mines and public transport in the second city of Plovdiv ran only to carry people to the daily opposition rally.
Sofia students marched with green-painted faces to protest that soaring inflation forced them to get nourishment from the sunlight like plants.
Plamen Dimitrov of the Confederation of Independent Trade Unions told the rally in Sofia that 250,000 workers had joined strikes and 1.5 million Bulgarians had taken part in some form of protest.

"It is obvious that since the UDF stepped up the protests, the Socialists' chances of forming a second government are decreasing every minute," Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told the rally.
Thursday was the 25th consecutive day of demonstrations calling for immediate elections and an end to rule by the Socialists, who won parliamentary polls in 1994.

President Petar Stoyanov, who warned on Wednesday that Bulgaria could default on its $10 billion foreign debt, met the European Union's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek in Brussels, who told him not to expect any new aid until political stability was restored.

On Wednesday Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee to head a new government, offered to stand down in the next three to five months and hold elections. The UDF declined, saying it wanted the vote at once.

Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov on Thursday wrote to each party in parliament inviting them for more talks. The Socialists have said they would like to form a coalition, but other parties have declined.
Under the constitution, Dobrev has until Tuesday to form a cabinet. Parvanov told reporters he was confident the cabinet would win enough votes in a secret ballot to be approved.
"I see no other way out of the current political crisis than to realise the mandate for a cabinet headed by Nikolai Dobrev," he said.
Outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December after months of criticism of his handling of the economy and the Socialists' defeat in November presidential elections.

The Socialists' youth wing had planned a potentially explosive counter-rally on Friday. One organiser said it had been cancelled after Sofia's UDF mayor set limitations on the route, but Kostov said he expected it to go ahead.
"We have heard that 100 buses will bring about 5,000 Socialist supporters to Sofia," he said.
"Everyone understands that they are clearly looking for a clash but we shall not allow this to happen."
Outgoing defence minister Dimitar Pavlov told reporters he was convinced the army would not become involved in the political standoff.
Influential business conglomerate Multigroup expressed support for Stoyanov's efforts to find a compromise.

But in the latest sign of impending economic collapse, state gas firm Bulgargas said it was reducing supplies to big industrial clients who had not paid their bills, because it was unable to pay its Russian supplier and was itself receiving less gas. It said domestic clients were not affected.

The lev, in freefall since the beginning of the year, closed lower than ever at 1,530-1,590 per dollar on the interbank market. Technicians had to reset banks' software to accept four-figure quotes when the lev fell below 1,000 for the first time on Tuesday.
